transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm not wasting your time with this, but... I guess I'm here because I've been having a little trouble lately. I'm in school for radiologic technology, which is great, I really like it. But... well, whenever I'm supposed to just sit still, like in the classroom or the radiology suite, I get this feeling like I'm completely crawling out of my skin. 

I know it probably sounds kind of silly for an 18-year-old to complain about sitting still, and I've really, really tried to just tough it out and be professional for months now. But I just can't seem to stop myself from shifting around constantly, or pacing, or, you know, finding some excuse to get up and move. I really want to do well in my program and not be a distraction to everyone else. Does that... does that make sense to come in for? I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by being here.
When did you first notice this feeling of not being able to sit still? Has this been something you've dealt with your whole life, or is it something that started more recently?

Um, well... I guess it's actually been going on for a really long time. I hope it's okay if I go back a bit? But, um, my parents actually still talk about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. 

I really don't want to sound like I was a troublemaker or a bad kid, I promise I wasn't trying to be disrespectful! But the teachers used to tell them that I was always out of my seat, or, you know, calling out in class, or rushing ahead to do assignments before they had even finished giving the directions. 

So... yeah, I guess that was happening way before middle school, even. It's definitely not just something that popped up recently since I started my radiology training. Is... is that the kind of information you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question right.

Besides the difficulty sitting still and the restlessness, have you also noticed that you have trouble concentrating or staying focused on tasks, even when you're interested in them? For example, do you find your mind wandering, or do you have difficulty keeping track of what someone is saying?

Um, actually... no, not really. I mean, I hope it's okay to say that, but I don't think I have a problem with focusing. Like, when I'm studying for my radiology classes or listening to a lecture, my mind doesn't really wander off. I can follow what the instructors are saying just fine, and I keep track of everything. It's really just the... the physical part, the needing to move, that bothers me. I'm sorry if that's not what you were expecting me to say! I just want to be completely honest so I'm not wasting your time. Does that make sense?

Besides school and your radiology training, have you noticed this restlessness and need to move affecting other areas of your life, like at home or in social situations? And has it caused problems for you in those settings?

Um, well, at home it's not too bad, I guess. I can kind of just do my own thing and move around if I need to. But... um, it has been causing some, well, some issues in the clinical part of my training. 

I really don't want to sound like a bad student, because I promise I'm trying so, so hard to do everything right. But my clinical evaluations have kind of... taken a hit lately. The supervisors, they said that my... my behavior, like the shifting and the pacing, they said it disrupts the patient flow and makes teamwork harder for everyone else. 

They actually... um, they put me on a formal remediation plan. I feel awful about it, I really do. I'm just so worried that if I can't figure out how to just be normal and sit still, it could cost me my place in the whole program. And I really love this field, I want to be a good tech. Is it okay that I'm telling you all this? I just really want to fix it so I don't let anyone down anymore.

When you're doing tasks that require attention, like studying or reading, do you find that you make careless mistakes, or do you sometimes have trouble organizing your thoughts or materials even though you can focus on what's being said?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I hope it's okay to say that, but I don't really struggle with those things. Like I said before, I can focus just fine, so studying and reading are okay. I'm pretty careful, so I don't really make careless mistakes, and I try really hard to keep all my materials organized. 

I really don't want to sound like I'm bragging or anything! I just... I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. The only thing I really struggle with is the physical part, the not being able to sit still. Is it okay that I don't have those other problems? I just want to make sure I'm being helpful.

You mentioned earlier that in elementary school you would call out in class and rush ahead before instructions were finished. Do you still find yourself doing things impulsively like that—interrupting people, blurting things out, or acting without thinking things through first?

Um, well... I guess I do still do that a little bit. I really try not to, because I know it's not polite, and I always feel so bad afterward. But sometimes... um, like when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step or, you know, asking me a question about a procedure, I'll just sort of jump in with the answer before they're even finished talking. 

I don't mean to be disrespectful or anything! I just get so eager to show them that I know the material, and then it just slips out. And then I realize I totally missed the second half of their sentence, which is usually the part that actually mattered. I always apologize right away when it happens. I really hope that doesn't make me sound like a terrible student... I am working on being better about waiting my turn to speak. Does that make sense, what I'm describing?

You mentioned you can focus well when studying and don't have trouble following lectures. But I want to ask more specifically: when you're doing everyday tasks or activities that aren't as interesting to you—like household chores, filling out forms, or repetitive work—do you find it hard to stick with those for very long, or do you tend to avoid them because they feel boring or tedious?

Um, no, not really. I mean... I hope it's okay to say this, but I'm actually pretty good about getting those kinds of things done. I know chores and forms aren't super fun, but I just sort of power through them, you know? 

I really try to be responsible and help out around the house, so I make sure I finish whatever I start. Even if it's tedious, I can stick with it. I don't avoid them or anything like that. I just... I want to make sure I'm doing what I'm supposed to do. Is it okay that I don't have a problem with that stuff either? I hope I'm still giving you the kind of answers you need.

When you're working on something on your own—like a project or assignment where you have to organize your own time and steps—do you ever find it hard to get started, or do you sometimes lose track of where you are in the process even though you're physically able to sit and work on it?

Um, no, I don't think so. I actually... well, I hope this doesn't sound like I'm not trying to be helpful, but I'm pretty good at managing my own projects. 

Like with my assignments for my radiology classes, I always make sure I know exactly what needs to be done. I don't really have trouble getting started, and I'm pretty careful about following the steps so I don't lose track of where I am. I just... I really want to do a good job and make sure I'm staying on top of everything. I'm sorry if that's not the answer you were looking for! I just want to make sure I'm giving you an accurate picture. Is it alright that I manage my time okay?

inference_history.note: Initial presentation with prominent restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, constant need for movement, and fidgeting in structured settings (classroom, clinical environment). Primary consideration is ADHD (Combined, Predominantly Hyperactive-Impulsive, or Unspecified type). Generalized Anxiety Disorder and depressive disorders included as differential diagnoses given the patient's distress and mention of 'toughing it out,' though hyperactivity symptoms are more prominent at this stage.
